posts.text:
Americans don't use WhatsApp because of a decision Apple made in 2013. We only know about it because the emails came out in court, and the whole thing came down to keeping your kids off Android.

It started with Eddy Cue, the guy who runs Apple's services. That April he emailed the team saying Apple really needed to put iMessage on Android. Google was reportedly trying to buy WhatsApp for $1 billion at the time, and Cue's pitch was that Apple already had the best messaging app, so why not make it the one the whole world used.

Craig Federighi, Apple's software chief, shut it down.

He asked how Apple was supposed to get Android users to leave WhatsApp when they didn't even have iPhone friends. So back in 2013, the guy running iPhone software was basically admitting WhatsApp already owned everybody who didn't have an iPhone. Then he got to what he was actually worried about. iMessage on Android would remove "an obstacle to iPhone families giving their kids Android phones."

Phil Schiller, Apple's longtime marketing boss, backed him up in another email thread in 2016, writing that putting iMessage on Android would hurt Apple more than help it. None of this was public until Epic sued Apple and the emails got pulled into evidence in 2021.

Now look at what that does to WhatsApp. The entire reason WhatsApp exists is that it works on any phone, so it wins wherever group chats are a mix of iPhones and Androids. Apple went the other direction on purpose. For years, every Android user in an American group chat showed up as a green bubble and their videos came through blurry, and the fix everybody landed on was buying another iPhone.

Tim Cook pretty much said this out loud in 2022. A reporter at a conference told him he couldn't send videos to his mom because she had an Android, and Cook told him to buy his mom an iPhone.

And it worked about as well as anything Apple has ever done. Nearly 9 in 10 American teenagers own an iPhone, and iPhones were 75% of phones sold at the big three US carriers in early 2026. If almost everyone you text has the same phone, an app whose whole selling point is working across phones has nothing to offer you.

Worldwide, Apple only sells about 1 in 5 phones. Most of the world's group chats stayed mixed, so they ended up on the one app that ran on everything, and WhatsApp blew past 3 billion users. Meta says more than 100 million Americans use it now too.

Apple finally added RCS texting with Android in 2024 and turned on encryption for it this May, and they still kept those messages green.

Apple basically let WhatsApp have the rest of the planet so it could keep American teenagers.

posts.text:
🇺🇸🇮🇷 Trump could lose Congress and STILL ESCALATE the war with Iran.

I spoke with Michael Tracey as Americans headed to the polls, and he challenged an assumption I've been hearing a lot lately.

That a crushing Republican defeat would force Trump to reconsider his Iran policy.

Michael isn't so sure.

He believes Trump is increasingly concerned with how history will remember his presidency. And after launching a war against Iran, walking away without a decisive victory might be something he's simply unwilling to accept.

Which raises an uncomfortable possibility.

Could Trump use the final two months of Republican control in Congress to launch another offensive before Democrats take over?

We also discussed Tucker Carlson's warning about a possible nuclear strike, although neither of us has evidence that Trump has decided to pursue one.

And Michael offered a rather interesting perspective on Trump's sudden suggestion that he might end American aid to Israel.

Even if the roughly $4 billion in annual assistance disappears, Washington has OTHER ways to provide military support. Ending one funding arrangement wouldn't necessarily end the relationship.

We also got into the possibility of an Iranian attack during election day, whether Democrats would actually impeach Trump, and why Michael thinks Texas could elect a Democratic senator.

I pushed back on his pessimism about Iran.

I still believe Trump could recognize that another military offensive would make an already difficult situation worse and choose a diplomatic exit.

Michael's concern is that Trump may care more about securing a historic victory than admitting the limits of American military power.

And the election could make that decision considerably more urgent.

@mtracey

I spoke with Emily Jashinsky as Americans headed to the polls, and she raised a rather uncomfortable possibility for Republicans.

What if the polls are actually UNDERESTIMATING how badly they could lose?

Emily believes pollsters may be overlooking former Trump supporters who voted for cheaper living costs and an end to foreign wars.

Instead, they're paying more at the pump and watching America fight another war in the Middle East.

And Trump's sudden change in messaging is interesting.

He's now talking about cutting American aid to Israel and negotiating peace with Iran, just as Republicans risk losing BOTH chambers of Congress.

But Emily questions whether voters will believe him, let alone whether he'll follow through.

We also discussed Michigan's El-Sayed–Rogers race, where support for Israel could become an electoral LIABILITY, Tucker Carlson's growing break with Trump, and the possibility of a serious third-party challenge.

There's also growing concern among administration officials about what a Democratic Congress could investigate.

What stayed with me was Emily's argument that the Iran war didn't create Trump's problems. It made everything his voters were already frustrated about MUCH harder to ignore.

And at this point, another campaign promise might not be enough.

🚨  Jesus Owono ‘I’m Truly Sorry After Accidental Challenge Claims Miguel’s Life:

"My heart is heavy beyond words right now. My phone has been ringing nonstop, filled with messages, and I kept asking myself what was happening only to learn the devastating news that Miguel has passed away.

This tragedy stems from the incident on the football pitch, when my knee made contact with his chest during a challenge. I need the world to hear this clearly: I am truly and deeply sorry. No apology, no matter how sincere or repeated, can ever bring Miguel back. That reality is something I will carry with me for the rest of my life.

Football is a physical game. As a player, my only intention in that moment was to stop the opposition from scoring and protect my team’s goal. What happened was never meant to harm Miguel. It was a pure football accident one that none of us could have predicted would end this way.

Since the news broke, I have been receiving threats and harsh messages. Still, nothing anyone says can match the pain I already feel. I am devastated. Right now I am not sure I will ever be able to step onto a professional pitch again, because I do not know if I will ever fully heal from knowing that my action, however unintentional, led to this loss.

It is heartbreaking to live with the knowledge that I was involved in the moment that took Miguel from us. The pain is real, deep, and constant.

To Miguel’s family, friends, teammates, and everyone who loved him: I am so sorry. My thoughts and prayers are with you. May his memory be a blessing, and may he rest in peace."
